stimulus.title: Jumping onto a merry-go-round
stimulus.html: A playground merry-go-round is a uniform disk of mass M and radius R (I = ½MR², given) that turns on a vertical axle. It starts at rest. A child of mass m runs along a line tangent to its rim at speed v and jumps on at the rim. Model the child as a point object.

y.label: Angular momentum of the child-merry-go-round system

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the angular velocity ω of the merry-go-round and child just after the child jumps on. Express your answer in terms of m, M, R, v and physical constants, as appropriate. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

rubric.point: Starts from conservation of angular momentum about the axle for the child-merry-go-round system, L_before = L_after
accept: L_i = L_f with L = Iω and L = rmv sin θ

rubric.point: Writes the child’s initial angular momentum as mvR (lever arm R) and the final rotational inertia as ½MR² + mR²
Correct answer in the given quantities

parts.sample: For the child-merry-go-round system, take angular momentum about the axle. Before: the child moves along a line a perpendicular distance R from the axle, so L = mvR; the merry-go-round has none. After: they turn together with I = ½MR² + mR². L_before = L_after: mvR = (½MR² + mR²)ω, so ω = mv / ((½M + m)R) = 2mv / ((M + 2m)R).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The child has mass 30 kg and runs at 4.0 m/s. The merry-go-round has mass 120 kg and radius 1.5 m. Calculate ω.

rubric.point: Correct value with units, about 0.89 rad/s
accept: a value consistent with the student’s expression from part (a)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: After the child is on, friction at the axle exerts a constant torque of 20 N·m that slows the merry-go-round until it stops. On the axes provided, sketch the angular momentum of the child-merry-go-round system about the axle as a function of time, from just before the child jumps on (t = 0) until the merry-go-round stops. The jump takes a very short time.

rubric.point: A horizontal line from just before the jump through the jump (no jump, drop or slope at the moment the child lands)
accept: flat line at mvR through t = 0

rubric.point: After the jump, a straight line with negative slope (constant slope) down to zero, and zero afterward
accept: straight line sloping down, then flat at zero

parts.sample: The graph is a horizontal line at L = mvR = 180 kg·m²/s before and through the jump: during the brief jump, the only external torques on the system (axle friction, and gravity and the axle’s push along the axis) give negligible angular impulse. After the jump, L falls in a straight line, with slope −20 N·m, reaching zero and staying at zero.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate how long the merry-go-round takes to stop after the child jumps on.

rubric.point: Uses angular impulse equals change in angular momentum (or α = τ/I with ω = ω₀ + αt)

accept: a value consistent with the student’s ω from part (b)

parts.sample: The friction torque delivers angular impulse τΔt = ΔL. The system’s L just after the jump is mvR = (30 kg)(4.0 m/s)(1.5 m) = 180 kg·m²/s, and it falls to zero: Δt = L/τ = 180/20 = 9.0 s.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A student claims that the kinetic energy of the child-merry-go-round system is the same just before and just after the child jumps on. Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Correct justification: compares the energies (240 J before, about 80 J after) or argues that the child and rim end with the same speed, like a perfectly inelastic collision, so kinetic energy is converted to thermal energy
accept: K_before = ½mv² = 240 J, K_after = ½Iω² ≈ 80 J
objects stick together, so the collision is inelastic and K is lost

parts.sample: Disagree. Before: K = ½mv² = ½(30)(4.0)² = 240 J. After: K = ½Iω² = ½(202.5 kg·m²)(0.889 rad/s)² ≈ 80 J. Angular momentum about the axle is the same, but kinetic energy falls: the child and the rim end up moving together, like a perfectly inelastic collision, and the lost kinetic energy becomes thermal energy (and sound) as the child’s feet grip and slide on the platform.
